To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

BiP interacts with the J domain in the lumenal domain of Sec63, that this interaction is required for translocation, that the interaction depends on ATP hydrolysis by BiP, and that the J domain in BiP interacts with Sec63p, but the J domain in Ssa1p interacts with another protein, perhaps a second translocation component.

BiP, a molecular chaperone, is essential for posttranslational transport of proteins into the ER and that this function of BiP requires ATP hydrolyzing activity, an interaction with a J domain-containing protein, and a conformational change in BiP.

BiP interacts with a specific DnaJ protein in the lumen of the ER membrane and that this interaction, which is ATP dependent, is necessary for BiP to drive protein translocation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how molecular chaperones function in protein translocation.
understanding how molecular chaperones function in the cell.
the molecular mechanisms by which proteins cross the endoplasmically reticulum membrane and the mechanisms by which the cell controls the translocation of proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hsp70 family of molecular chaperones is essential for the translocation of nascent proteins into the endoplasmatic reticulum.
the specificity of chaperone action is dictated by the J domain of the partner chaperone, and the specificity of the J domain is dictated by the partner chaperones.
BiP is the only ER-resident hsc70 that can bind the J domain of the Sec63p and that the interaction of BiP and Sec63p is required to drive the protein translocation into yeast ER membrane.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the specificity of molecular chaperone function is dictated by their partners.
BiP is the only hsc70 that can interact with the J domain in the ER lumen and that this interaction is required for BiP function in translocation.

the hsc70 chaperone system is a complex, highly regulated machine that can interact with many different proteins and that the specificity and regulation of the system is determined by the interaction of hsc70 with DnaJ.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the molecular specificity required for the translocation of proteins into the ER is determined by the interactions between the lumenal hsp70, BiP, and the J domain of the membrane protein, Sec63p, and not by the cytosolic homologue of BiP, Ssa1p.
the specificity of the action of the molecular chaperone BiP is dictated by its interaction with the DnaJ homology domain of Sec63.
BiP and Ssa1p have very similar ATPase activity but different substrate binding specificity.
